entries.title: Sean Burke, Davis Martin will need to be durable for White Sox, who lose to Astros
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> are going to need <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/07/19/sean-burke-white-sox-toronto-davis-martin-starting-pitchers" target="_blank" >Sean Burke and Davis Martin</a> to be at their best to win the American League Central. That means Burke and Martin will have to breeze past their career highs in innings pitched while staying effective.</p><p>The foundation for them to do that was built last year, when both set their personal marks, albeit when the stakes were much lower.</p><p>On their way to their third straight 100-loss season, the Sox got 142‰ innings from Martin and 134⅓ from Burke. As Martin said, both had “training wheels” on in 2025 because of their respective injury histories: Martin hadn’t pitched a full season since undergoing Tommy John surgery in 2023, and shoulder issues limited Burke in 2023 and 2024.</p><p>“Looking back, it was the best thing for us,” Martin told the Sun-Times on Saturday before the Sox lost to the Astros 4-1. “We had a solid workload last year, so throwing 170-180 innings isn’t going to be too over the top compared to going from 80 innings to 180.”</p><p>That many innings this year is possible for both. The Sox have 59 regular-season games left, and they hope a few more in October.</p><p>Through 20 starts, Martin already has pitched 111 innings. Like Martin did Friday, Burke ran into trouble in the sixth Saturday. After throwing five scoreless innings, Burke loaded the bases with no outs. Isaac Paredes singled to right to bring in two runs, and when Braden Montgomery overran the ball, a third scored.</p><p>The inning was decisive, spoiling an otherwise-solid night for Burke, who was beaten by Hunter Brown’s seven scoreless innings. Burke struck out 10 and didn’t look like a pitcher wearing down at 118⅓ innings.</p><p>“I [am] just taking care of my arm and the on-field results but also trying to stay consistent with my routine in between weeks, too,” Burke said.</p><p>The Sox certainly will monitor him and Martin, but innings limits are not in their future.</p><p>“You just need to be mindful between starts and having an idea of where they’re at, physically, mentally and those things,” manager Will Venable said. “But as far as innings go, that’s not something that’s going to limit us or drive what we do.”</p><p>Knowing that, it’s on the pitchers as much as anybody to stay on their programs to keep themselves on the mound.</p><p>Martin said he has introduced correctives from past back spasms and forearm problems to his regular schedule to try to avoid future issues. He made it past 80 innings healthy, which he couldn’t do last year, when he went on the injured list in June with a forearm strain, interrupting an otherwise durable 2025.</p><p>“The last two to three years have been a really good runway for me to figure out what has and hasn’t worked for me in the past,” Martin said.</p><p>Even if Martin’s methods continue working, it doesn’t mean he’ll feel great the rest of the year. Martin said he spoke with former Sox pitchers Lance Lynn, Martin Perez and Dylan Cease about throwing a lot of innings, and they shared what worked for them.</p><p>“The overview is that no one feels good,” Martin said. “No one feels 100% in October and September. So that is the biggest thing for me mentally, just thinking ‘Hey, you’re going to have to push through some stuff.’ I feel like we’ve already done that this year.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" name="list-4a0005"></a><div class="PageList-header" > <div class="PageList-header-title-wrap" > <div class="PageList-header-title"> <a class="" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="{borderColor=#dfdfdf, pageNumber=1, inverseColors=false, footerBgColor=#000000, bodyFont=font-3, items=[{type=Image, timestamp=1785026816000, wordCount=711, _styledTemplate=null, authors=[{authorPageUrl=https://chicago.suntimes.com/barry-m-bloom, name=[{items=[Barry M. entries.title: Motorcyclist dies after crash on DuSable Lake Shore Drive in Lake View
entries.summary: <p>A motorcyclist was killed after crashing Saturday night on DuSable Lake Shore Drive in Lake View.</p><p>The 20-year-old man was driving north in the 2200 block of DuSable Lake Shore Drive around 7:22 p.m. when he lost control and struck a barrier, Chicago police said.</p><p>He fell over the barrier, into oncoming traffic and was struck by a car, police said.</p><p>The man suffered multiple injuries and was taken to Illinois Masonic Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, police said.</p><p>CPD’s Major Accidents Unit is investigating.</p>

entries.title: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert keeps her head down, picks her phone up
entries.summary: <p>This just in: WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert plans to text the players more.</p><p>That wasn't Engelbert's only takeaway from All-Star weekend, of course.</p><p>But the plan to "institute more frequent communication," as the former Deloitte CEO put it, stuck out.</p><p>The knock on Engelbert, who is facing mounting public criticism from league insiders, is that her relationship-building needs work. Players feel like they don't hear from her on a regular basis.</p><p>Asked to characterize the current relationship, four-time MVP A'ja Wilson repeated her standard line: She really only knows Engelbert from trophy handoffs.</p><p>Engelbert said she took that feedback this weekend. She's now realizing that players don't really read their emails. She's now realizing they might actually want to hear from her casually, a happy birthday text or check-in after an injury or milestone.</p><p>Is it too little, too late? Maybe. Multiple <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/wnba/story/_/id/49436321/wnba-2026-cathy-engelbert-commissioner-future-all-star-break" target="_blank" >reports</a> from ESPN and Sports Business Journal in recent weeks suggest many league insiders believe this might, or at least should, be her final year.</p><p>One thing most agree on: She has put the league on much more stable financial footing and got a CBA done that made players millionaires. But the office requires savvy in the personal, communication and PR side too.</p><p>Asked whether she plans to be commissioner in 2027, Engelbert gave her usual answer about keeping her head down.</p><p>"I'm so blessed to have to be at the helm of this league during this incredible hyper growth period," she said. "So I will continue to do my job, execute the strategy, because it has been working. Make sure we listen to the players, communicate with the players. Absolutely just love this league."</p><p>For now, she's still chugging away at the priorities: improving officiating, which has remained a pain point this season. Globalizing the game, a standard playbook for professional sports these days. And improving player security, which matters even more in a women's league, where players face disproportionately more threats.</p><p>The last point was the focus of the weekend. League leaders met with players to address the online harassment they increasingly receive. Mercury star Alyssa Thomas recently described death threats after her flagrant foul on Fever star Caitlin Clark. Aces star Chelsea Gray talked about receiving racial slurs from someone who had bet on one of her games.</p><p>Engelbert said the meeting was productive and that the league will invest in enhanced security personnel and protocols.</p><p>On officiating, Engelbert announced an improvement many have called for: Like the NBA, the WNBA will install a replay center for the 2027 season, helping on-court officials make more accurate and efficient decisions when reviewing plays.</p><p>There's still plenty of work to be done for the WNBA's infrastructure to match its quality of play. But the league keeps growing. Engelbert pointed out that 29 games have averaged more than 1 million viewers, up from 11 at this point last year. The All-Star Game set an attendance record with nearly 20,000 fans. </p><p>And the game itself was a delight, with a nice balance of style and comic interludes. Team Spoon, led by MVP Jonquel Jones, won 129-122. The young stars — Caitlin Clark, Olivia Miles, Paige Bueckers and Dominique Malonga — all dazzled.</p><p>As a whole, All-Star weekend painted the picture of a league that's thriving.</p><p>Engelbert is embattled, but she presided over a remarkable transformation: a league once on the margins, now fully mainstream. There's plenty to like about her legacy. If only she'd thought to institute the Texting Initiative a little sooner.</p>
entries.author: Alissa Hirsh

entries.title: MVPETE > Cy Skenes? Pete Crow-Armstrong dazzles as Cubs beat up October-type ace Paul Skenes
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH – <b>Paul Skenes</b> is the type of pitcher the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> are going to have to beat if they’re going to make a deep October run.</p><p>They showed they’re capable of taking it to the game’s best, tagging the Pirates’ ace and reigning NL Cy Young winner for five runs in an 11-0 blowout win Saturday.</p><p>It was another banner night for All-Star center fielder <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b>, who won two of his three showdowns with Skenes – his crushed RBI double off the wall started the scoring – and had four hits on the night, homering and coming a triple shy of his second cycle of the season.</p><p>“I love facing Paul,” Crow-Armstrong said of Skenes, a teammate both as a pre-teen and with Team USA in the World Baseball Classic. “He’s one of the best competitors in our sport. I admire that the most about him.</p><p>“I love how he goes about his business. It’s fun to watch that behind the scenes when you get to be in the same clubhouse as him. Taking that personal experience into today with me and into any matchup with him, it’s fun.”</p><p>Skenes is good as big league arms come, once again a candidate for the sport’s top pitching award in a crowded NL field.</p><p>But Crow-Armstrong is having a spectacular season, making the case that he is – as the award states – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >the most valuable player in baseball</a>. He came into Saturday leading the game’s position players with 6.6 fWAR.</p><p>“The best leadoff hitter,” lefty starter <b>Shota Imanaga</b> said through an interpreter. “He can get extra-base hits, he can hit a homer, he can get on, he can steal.</p><p>“If you’re the opposing pitcher and you’re facing him to start a game, that’s tough.”</p><p><b>From Steel City to the North Side</b></p><p>Left fielder <b>Ian Happ</b> walked Saturday, extending his on-base streak in his hometown to a remarkable 43 games, the longest such streak in PNC Park’s history.</p><p>A night earlier, Happ did it all in an extra-inning Cubs win, making big plays with his bat, with his glove and on the base paths.</p><p>“Ian’s amazing,” lefty starter <b>Matthew Boyd</b> said. “It speaks to what he is as a player, what he means to this team.”</p><p>Whether Happ’s 10th season on the North Side is his last – <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/23/seiya-suzuki-walk-up-music-frank-sinatra-my-way-free-agent-contract-home-runs-lineup-payroll" >like outfield-mate <b>Seiya Suzuki</b></a>, Happ’s slated to hit free agency after the season – his experience with the organization has proven valuable inside the Cubs’ clubhouse.</p><p>“He truly embodies what it means to be a Cub,” Boyd said. “He plays the game the right way. You hear his ovation every time he jogs out to left field, from the bleachers. … Some of those things might seem irrelevant to some people, but it is special.</p><p>“He knows the gravity of putting on those pinstripes and what it means to the city and the fans.</p><p>“He’s a direct connection to that 2016 team, too, and he got to play around a lot of champions. Whenever … you get to be around championship players, that stuff wears off on you. He carries himself like a pro, and you can’t put a price tag on that. It’s valuable to all of us.”</p><p><b>Shota shoves</b></p><p>Imanaga threw six shutout innings Saturday. He’s been excellent since a sour four-start stretch earlier this summer, with a 2.00 ERA in his last eight outings, a boon for an injury-plagued Cubs pitching staff.</p><p>“The chances we’ve had when he’s been on the mound this whole year have been plentiful,” Crow-Armstrong said. “He’s pitching exactly like he is capable of, and he’s definitely got some more where that came from, too.”</p>

entries.title: Teresa Weatherspoon, fired by the Sky in 2024, 'absolutely' wants a second crack at coaching in the WNBA
entries.summary: <p>Former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky</a> coach Teresa Weatherspoon didn’t like it when members of the media called her by her first name during press conferences and interviews. “Coach,” “Coach Spoon” or even just “Spoon” was the way she felt it should be. Using her first name was too familiar or not quite reverent enough, seemed to be her position on the matter.</p><p>I didn’t like that she didn’t like it. Or more like I didn’t care. I rolled my eyes so hard at it, they might still be rolling.</p><p>But you know what? I can be a real ninny. As I learned just this weekend — <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky-and-wnba/2024/09/26/sky-fire-coach-teresa-weatherspoon-after-one-season" target="_blank" >nearly two years after the Sky fired her</a> — Weatherspoon’s objection wasn’t about ego or hubris. It was nothing more than where she comes from and how she was raised.</p><p>I picked this up watching her seven-month-old appearance on former Sky star Angel Reese’s podcast, “pologetically Angel.” In it, Weatherspoon described her childhood in rural east Texas, in a tiny town where the two most oft-spoken words were “sir” and “ma’am.” All adults were addressed that way, according to Weatherspoon, who is 60. It wasn’t an expectation but rather a demand.</p><p>Maybe I’d have figured this out sooner had she been here for longer than one season before the Sky showed her the door. One year isn’t much time to get to know anybody in any setting, especially if you’re a know-it-all columnist showing up around a team only every now and then.</p><p>Weatherspoon was at the United Center Saturday in the capacity of “general manager” of one of the WNBA All-Star teams — a nod to her excellence as one of the 30-year-old league’s first star players — so I asked her about it. No, not about the name thing. About the kicked-to-the-curb-after-only-one-year thing.</p><p>“Nothing stops the show,” she said twice. “I’m not the only person in the world that this has happened to, you know? I’m not.</p><p>“But one thing about me, it doesn’t hold me down. Nothing holds me down and I move forward, and that’s the most important thing is moving forward and knowing who you are and what you bring. … No one can stop that.”</p><p>Weatherspoon has a job coaching in the Unrivaled league, but she would “absolutely” like to get another crack at the WNBA.</p><p>She won a national championship as a point guard at Louisiana Tech, where she later took the reins as coach. She was the WNBA’s first assists and steals champion as a rookie and became a five-time All-Star. Before going to the Sky, she was an NBA assistant coach with the Pelicans. But when it comes to being a WNBA head coach, all she has on her résumé is a one-and-done with the Sky in 2024.</p><p>Talk about a kick in the gut. It had to hurt.</p><p>“It was a tremendous shock for me,” Weatherspoon said on Reese’s podcast.</p><p>The stuff of coaching and leading has coursed through Weatherspoon’s veins since she first picked up a ball, she recalls.</p><p>“I love it,” she said. “I love just studying it. I love the grit and grind of it all, and then the wit — like how quickly [things] have to happen — and the challenge of it all, and then playing chess. If you’re playing checkers, you’re going to get beat.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <blockquote </div> </div></div><p>Weatherspoon meant a great deal to Reese and still does. At All-Star media day on Friday, Weatherspoon surfaced in a crowd of reporters around Reese and asked a couple of admiring questions — neither having to do with herself — but Reese took it as a chance to reflect praise onto her first WNBA coach.</p><p>“Coming into my rookie year, I didn’t know what I was going to be,” Reese said. “I think you put a lot of everything into me, from energy to love to support. I was the No. 7 pick and didn’t [know if] I was going to do anything … [but] you put a lot of conscience into me and I’m thankful for that.”</p><p>The player-coach relationship didn’t last, at least not officially, but they continued to talk “every day” during Reese’s second and final year with the Sky, according to Reese.</p><p>And after news broke that the Sky had fired Weatherspoon, the first text and first call came from Reese.</p><p>Weatherspoon seems to have gotten over the sting.</p><p>“I don’t want to sit in a place where I’m holding a grudge,” she said on the podcast. “I can’t do that [or else] you win. entries.title: It took awhile, but Andruw Jones, Carlos Beltran, Jeff Kent made Baseball Hall of Fame
entries.summary: <p>COOPERSTOWN, N.Y. — If there’s a theme that runs through the induction ceremony Sunday for the National Baseball Hall of Fame on the stage behind the Clark Sports Center, it’s that the three players had to wait.</p><p>There’s no Derek Jeter, Ichiro Suzuki or Mariano Rivera, who all played for one team. No first-time ballot inductees in this group.</p><p>It still will be a singular moment, one Carlos Beltran wondered if he’d ever experience. He made it on his third try in January, receiving votes on 84.2% of the 425 ballots filed by eligible members of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America. Andruw Jones, in his ninth try, earned 78.4% of the vote. The baseline is 75%. Jeff Kent was elected last year by the 16-member Contemporary Baseball Era Committee after 10 years when the BBWAA passed.</p><p>“I appreciate all the reporters that voted for me,” Beltran said. “And for those who didn’t vote for me, I also respect their perspective, how they made their judgment. That being said, I’m going to enjoy this moment.”</p><p>Beltran was entangled in the Astros’ sign-stealing scandal of 2017. The Astros defeated the Dodgers in a seven-game World Series that is forever tainted. The active players were given immunity during the MLB investigation that followed. The coaches, manager and executive were not.</p><p>He was no longer active. On Nov. 19, 2019, he was named manager of the Mets. Then he lost that chance. When MLB issued its scathing report on Jan. 13, 2020, Beltran was the only player named. He was retired and had fallen between the cracks.</p><p>Beltran, who played 20 seasons from 1998 to 2017 for seven teams, including the Yankees and Mets, wondered if he’d ever get into the Hall.</p><p>“It was a possibility,” Beltran said. “You know what? Everything is a possibility in life. I have to say when the Astros situation happened, at the beginning, the first couple of years, there were people who didn’t vote for me, but they voted for me after three years. The question will be: What changed for them? What changed their mind to reward me to get elected to the Hall of Fame?”</p><p>Times change. People are sometimes forgiven for their transgressions.</p><p>Jones played 17 seasons with five teams, but he was best known for his first 12 as a 10-time Gold Glove-winning center fielder for the Braves. During his last five seasons, he gained weight and nearly fell off the map playing for four teams — the Dodgers, Rangers, White Sox and Yankees. He finished his career in Japan. Jones was a .254 lifetime hitter with 434 homers. In those last five big-league seasons, he hit .210 with only 66 homers.</p><p>Near the end of his 10-year tenure on the BBWAA ballot, the writers had a change of heart.</p><p>Jones is now one of six players from those 1990s Braves to make the Hall of Fame, including Tom Glavine, Greg Maddux, John Smoltz, Chipper Jones and Fred McGriff. Late manager Bobby Cox and general manager John Schuerholz also are in the Hall. All of Jones’ former teammates are here for the ceremony.</p><p>“We all sat down at a round table [Friday],” Jones said. “They called to congratulate me. They kept saying, ‘Be patient. You’re going to be there.’ It was a battle for nine years. You try not to think about it because life keeps going.”</p><p>Kent played 17 years for six teams and despite having the most homers for a second baseman — 351 of his 377 homers playing that position — never earned any traction on the BBWAA ballot. He peaked at 46.5% in his 10th and final season. But last year, a 16-member era committee picked him as the only electee from the eight players on the ballot. He needed 12 votes. Kent said Saturday he felt like a “cool cat” a day before making his speech.</p><p>“I can handle it, so right now I’m good,” he said. But Sunday?</p><p>“I’m going to have anxiety at the level that I’m going to need some drugs to calm me down,” he added.</p><p>For these guys, it has been that kind of roller-coaster experience for years.</p><p><b>2026 BASEBALL HALL OF FAME INDUCTEES</b></p><p><b>• Carlos Beltran</b>, center fielder<br><b>• Andruw Jones</b>,<b> </b>center fielder<br><b>• Jeff Kent</b>,<b> </b>second baseman<br><b>• Joe Buck</b>,<b> </b>Ford C. Frick Award<br><b>• Paul Hoynes</b>,<b> </b>BBWAA Career<br>Excellence<br><b>• Bill White</b>,<b> </b>Buck O’Neil<b> </b>Lifetime<br>Achievement<br></p>

entries.title: Fire drop second straight since returning from break
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Nicolas Fernandez scored a goal for the third consecutive game, Agustin Ojeda and Malachi Jones each added a goal and New York City FC beat the Fire 3-1 on Saturday night.</p><p>Joel Waterman scored his first goal this season for the Fire (8-6-2), who have lost back-to-back games after a three-game winning streak before going on the World Cup break. Both losses have come since the addition of Polish star Robert Lewandowski.</p><p>Ojeda, on the counter-attack, ran onto a through ball played ahead by Andrés Perea and bent a shot from the right side of the area off the back post and into the net to make it 2-1 in the 29th.</p><p>Fernandez blasted a first-touch shot, off a clearance played by Jack Elliott, from 25 yards out to open the scoring in the 10th minute.</p><p>Waterman tied it at 1-all in the 21st minute. Anton Saletros played a free kick from the right sideline that was redirected by Ojeda’s header at the front post, and Waterman tapped it inside the back post from point-blank range.</p><p>Jones' first goal since 2024 gave NYCFC a two-goal lead in the 41st minute. Perea played a ball ahead to Ojeda, who tapped a cross from the right side of the area to Jones for a first-touch finish from point-blank range.</p><p>Matt Freese had FOUR saves for NYCFC (7-6-4).<br></p>

entries.title: Brother Rice DL Brayden Parks is third top-10 player from Illinois headed to Irish in 2027 recruiting cycle
entries.summary: <p>Notre Dame football’s recruiting push in Chicago continues to pay big dividends.</p><p>On Thursday, Brother Rice defensive lineman Brayden Parks announced his commitment to the Fighting Irish on CBS Sports College Football’s YouTube channel.</p><p>Parks, whose godfather is former Vocational and Notre Dame star Chris Zorich, is the third top-10 player from Illinois landed by Irish coach Marcus Freeman in the 2027 recruiting cycle.</p><p>All are from the Catholic League — St. Patrick defensive lineman David Folrunsho and Mount Carmel linebacker Roman Igwebuike are the others — and all are consensus top-200 players nationally. Parks is the No. 10 player in Illinois, the No. 24 defensive lineman and the No. 199 player nationally in the 247Sports composite rankings.</p><p>The Irish have been stocking up on local defensive linemen in recent years. Already on the roster are Simeon’s Christopher Burgess Jr., IC Catholic’s Dominik Hulak and York’s Joe Reiff.</p><p>Parks, a 6-3, 305-pounder, had more than 40 offers and cut his list of potential destinations to Notre Dame and Oregon.</p><p>He talked about his recruiting on the YouTube video: “It’s a long time coming, but at the end of the day, it’s a blessing.”</p><p>His wish list?</p><p>“I was looking for a team that’s going to be in the playoffs every year, a team that has a chance of winning a national championship.”</p><p>He also was looking for a strong connection with his coaches, who will include Freeman, defensive line coach Charlie Partridge and assistant defensive line coach Nick Sebastian.</p><p>“Just talking to coach Freeman, it shows he cares [about me], not just as a football player but as a person,” Parks said. “I’ve known coach Sebastian since I started my recruiting process about four years ago and then coach [Partridge] came into it this January.”</p><p>Parks is coming off a productive season for the Class 7A champion Crusaders. He had 61 tackles, 7œ sacks, 23 tackles for loss and an interception en route to being named Defensive Player of the Year in the rugged CCL/ESCC Blue.</p><p>National recruiting analyst Clint Cosgrove sees a bright future for Parks at Notre Dame.</p><p>“The kid is an absolute beast,” Cosgrove said. “The size/frame combination is very rare. It’s hard to find those big defensive tackles who can push those double-teams back and also rush the passer.</p><p>“He’s the complete package.”</p><p>And as good as Parks is now, Cosgrove said, “he’s just going to get bigger, better, stronger. . . . His best football is in front of him.”</p><h3>More on 2027 prospects</h3><p>With Parks picking Notre Dame, the vast majority of the state’s top prospects will be committed when high school practice starts Aug. 5. That doesn’t mean there won’t be any more recruiting news coming, though. In every cycle, some recruits flip schools, decommitting from one and picking another.</p><p>And there are still a few high-level prospects who haven’t made a decision. The state’s top-ranked uncommitted player in the rising senior class is No. 23 Lawrence Carr, a receiver from Kenwood.</p><p>The early signing period for football will be Dec. 4-6, with the traditional signing day scheduled for Feb. 5, 2027.<br></p>

entries.title: Forecasting Blackhawks' lines with Patrick Kane and Bowen Byram — but without Connor Bedard
entries.summary: <p>With Connor Bedard's and Patrick Kane's signings complete, the Blackhawks' roster for the 2026-27 season is likely set.</p><p>Restricted free agents Kevin Korchinski and Ethan Del Mastro still need contracts, but they won't be significant. The Hawks' news cycle will probably be slow and stay slow until rookie camp leads into training camp in September.</p><p>In the meantime, coach Jeff Blashill and his staff can begin sketching rough drafts of lineups for the start of this season, which will be complicated by Bedard not returning from shoulder surgery until November.</p><p>Here's an equally rough forecast of what those forward lines and defensive pairings might look like:</p><h3><b>Forward lines</b></h3><p>Who will fill in for Bedard as the first-line center in October? That's a burning question the Hawks will need to figure out in camp. </p><p>Once Bedard returns, the lines figure to change significantly, although the odds are somebody else will be injured by then.</p><p><b>Roman Kantserov — Frank Nazar — Patrick Kane</b></p><p>Whether Kantserov will look like a promising rookie or a fully ready-to-go star — building upon his 36-goal season in Russia last season — is another burning question. General manager Kyle Davidson hasn't shied away from setting high expectations for him.</p><p>Meanwhile, it's pretty easy to predict what Kane will be: a savvy, charismatic playmaker with defensive flaws and decreasing speed.</p><p>It will be thrilling to see Kane eventually set up Bedard goals, but he also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/24/patrick-kane-blackhawks-return-playoffs-connor-bedard-kyle-davidson?_gl=1*iqw19k*_up*MQ..*_ga*MTM4MDcyNjI2Ny4xNzg0OTI3Nzkx*_ga_K0F0MB46T8*czE3ODQ5Mjc3OTAkbzEkZzAkdDE3ODQ5Mjc3OTAkajYwJGwwJGgw" target="_blank" >brought up</a> Nazar on Friday. They've skated together this summer, and Nazar has impressed Kane enough to make him wonder about them playing together.</p><p>The Hawks would love to see Nazar start this season like he did last season (with 11 points in 10 games) and maintain that momentum longer in the first year of his big seven-year contract.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Following another developmental leap this summer, he could round out the top six.</p><p><b>Teuvo Teravainen — Oliver Moore — Ryan Greene</b></p><p>When Bedard returns, Moore may get pushed to the wing, but Bedard's absence presents Moore with a golden opportunity to grab hold of a checking-line center role. </p><p>Moore's defensive analytics were solid last season and he <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/14/blackhawks-oliver-moore-studying-nhl-sharpening-brain-summer" target="_blank" >expressed interest</a> in molding himself into a defensive specialist, but his season-ending injury prevented him from finishing the season in Jason Dickinson's old spot. That tryout comes now.</p><p>Teravainen, coming off a subpar season, and Greene, coming off a rookie season in which he played a role (on the first line) that nobody expects him to keep long-term, aren't easy to slot on the depth chart. They're both intelligent players, though, so maybe they could join forces on a defensive line.</p><p><b>Cole Smith — Ryan Donato — Jordan Greenway</b></p><p>The Hawks sought to add more grit and physicality this summer and did so with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/01/blackhawks-ian-cole-smith-nhl-free-agency-ilya-mikheyev" target="_blank" >Smith</a> and Greenway, two large forwards who aren't afraid to dish hits or drop gloves.</p><p>Blashill cast Donato into a bottom-six role last season and isn't likely to change that stance, although Donato could potentially switch places with Greene.</p><p>Landon Slaggert and Andrew Mangiapane, as it stands now, appear to be the forward extras. Mangiapane could be Rockford-bound at some point, as he's essentially guaranteed to clear waivers due to his $3.6 million salary-cap hit.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-credit"><p>Michael Reaves/Getty Images</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Defensive pairings</b></h3><p>The pairings are tricky to predict because the Hawks have five left-handed vs. two right-handed defensemen, although both new left-handed additions — Bowen Byram and Ian Cole — have experience playing both sides.</p><p>There are a couple ways the Hawks could approach this. They could balance out the pairings with one aggressive, puck-moving defenseman and one conservative, stay-at-home defenseman on each one, or they could unite like-minded defensemen to create, for example, one shutdown pairing.</p><p><b>Alex Vlasic — Bowen Byram</b></p><p>This top duo assumes the Hawks opt for more balanced pairings and that Byram is the lefty who shifts to the right. One way or another, Byram will likely lead the unit in ice time by several minutes per game over everyone else.</p><p>Vlasic's development has plateaued somewhat over the last two seasons. He and Louis Crevier, his most common partner last season, faced brutal matchups and disrupted plays well enough with their long reaches, but they struggled to exit the defensive zone after doing so.</p><p>Byram's puck-moving abilities could help Vlasic with that, while Vlasic could cover for Byram when he eagerly jumps into rushes. </p><p>Ultimately, the defense's success will depend on Byram quickly becoming a No. 1 defenseman and seizing this <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/07/01/blackhawks-bowen-byram-contract-nhl-defensemen-free-agency" target="_blank" >opportunity</a> he waited for. He needs to dominate his minutes no matter who he's playing with.</p><p><b>Wyatt Kaiser — Sam Rinzel</b></p><p>Kaiser's pairing with Artyom Levshunov was a major disappointment last season, as they were outscored 30-10 during their ice time together.</p><p>Kaiser himself was a bright spot, though, as the Hawks actually outscored opponents 39-36 when he wasn't with Levshunov. Duncan Keith is a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/10/blackhawks-defense-duncan-keith-wyatt-kaiser-artyom-levshunov-hall-of-fame" target="_blank" >believer</a> in Kaiser, too. </p><p>Perhaps playing him with a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/blackhawks/2026/04/26/blackhawks-sam-rinzel-weight-gain-summer-plan-nhl-rookie-season" target="_blank" >strengthened Rinzel</a> would work? Their stats weren't bad together last season.</p><p><b>Ian Cole — Artyom Levshunov</b></p><p>Cole has quietly delivered solid results everywhere throughout his journeyman career, making him a potentially good, stabilizing partner for Levshunov (or Rinzel).</p><p>"If I can handle my business and bring a consistent product night after night, it's something the coaches and teammates can rely on," Cole said earlier this month. "[We'll] figure out how we can meld all these different skill sets and personalities together."</p><p>Levshunov needs to take a large development step this summer. He has the raw tools to do so, and his decision to spend most of it in Chicago rather than Florida should help, but only time will tell if he has.</p><p>Korchinski is no longer waiver-exempt and likely figures to start the season as the seventh defenseman, but the Hawks will need to find ways to rotate him in. Del Mastro will also require waivers and may well find himself on them at the end of camp.</p><p><b>Goalies: Spencer Knight, Arvid Soderblom</b></p><p>Knight could be slated for one of the larger workloads in the NHL this season, while Soderblom holds a tenuous grip on the backup job over still waivers-exempt Drew Commesso.</p>

entries.title: WNBA's Sophie Cunningham is the woman of the moment
entries.summary: <p>She’s not here, but she’s here. She won’t be seen on the court during the events of WNBA All-Star Weekend or in the game, but she’ll be felt. Presence (not pomp) and circumstance carry substance, as they often apprentice popularity.</p><p>Sophie the Great. The protector to her teammate’s (Caitlin Clark) perceived privilege and pedestal. The Billie Eilish to Taylor Swift. The bad ‘‘girl.’’ Hailed as a ‘‘hero’’ and ‘‘anti-Megan Rapinoe’’ by Clay Travis, Sophie Cunningham, in all of her anti-trans misquoted splendor, feminized alt-femmephilia, anti-put in anyone’s mislabeled box, has reached ‘‘it’’ status.</p><p>Dana White and Morgan Wallen fanboy alignments. The MAGA Barbie moniker. Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue fame. It all fits for the heaven-sent tsunami of a MAGA-propagated athlete being catapulted into the spotlight as the new embodiment and human brand image of a racially charged, capitalistic and nationalistic movement.</p><p>She’s perfect.</p><p>A one-woman referendum. The ‘‘I stand on what I said’’ controversy about her overall beliefs against transgender athletes participating in women’s sports. (Where she also said she believes her stance is ‘‘common sense.’’) The controversy surrounding the WNBA players’ union gangster-ing the rights of her ‘‘finger pointing’’ viral image that became (so far) the meme of this sports-as-political-messaging summer. Her ‘‘controversial’’ adidas signature PE color way (not signature sneaker, big difference; plus, Satou Sabally has the same Crazy Energy adidas model PE named after her dropping, but no one is making a big deal about that?) that impelled Jemele Hill to capture Cunningham’s ‘‘moment’’ to perfection: ‘‘Rarely do you see someone who’s career average is eight points per game receive this level of attention. I think she’s fiery, outspoken, she’s very aware of being a media darling right now and looking to capitalize on this, and understands that entertainment is a part of her game.’’</p><p>The controversy last year that swirled around the ‘‘hurtful’’ and false allegations that she publicly had to answer about a lawsuit claiming she had an affair when she played for the Mercury with Suns CEO Josh Bartelstein.</p><p>Is this meteoric Sophie moment ephemeral? Doubt it. Especially if she plays it right, plays well and stays in front of who she is before the outside world (her followers and Clark ‘‘enablers’’) get in front of her for her. She, more than Caitlin, is positioning herself to be the face of a movement. We are watching a player in real time find her calling while a calling within society finds her.</p><p>She just might be the only living being now with more hype around her than Jimothy.</p><p>She’s being positioned to represent a side of one culture the same way Allen Iverson was for an entire other side of a whole other culture. But she doesn’t have the MVP or potential Hall of Fame career (yet) to match. The fringe version, the aesthetic version. The one that, in basketball circles, has nothing to do with basketball. One, though, that is very real and carries with it power that has the power to keep her game secondary. Transformative power.</p><p>Despite her very much centrist and down-the-middle public statement on her political affiliation and association — she was quoted in an ESPN feature as saying, ‘‘I’m very much in the middle. I agree with things on both sides, disagree with things on both sides. And that’s all I’ve ever said about my political beliefs. But people love to assume.’’ — Cunningham’s ‘‘presence’’ and ‘‘acceptance’’ of where society seems to be placing her and what that placement represents seem to identify with something different.</p><p>Something she has chosen not to claim, acknowledge or officially embrace but may soon no longer be her decision to make. Making her ‘‘Screw that, I’m gonna be me’’ approach an easy target for an ideology desperate to find and use a female athlete (specifically, a binary, White, outspoken basketball player) as their un-woke mouthpiece.</p><p>Something, apparently, she’s going to allow society to choose for her about her. Which can be a dangerous game to play. Whom she really is and whom she’s presented and positioned to be may soon no longer be Sophie’s choice. Unlike the fan base that has adopted her, the ‘‘game’’ doesn’t discriminate when it gets to the level Cunningham’s entering.</p><p>Columbian (Mo.) Sophie. The spicy one. She got the jazz. (Oh, that one will go way over most of y’all’s heads.) CC22’s 4:44. Her conscious. As they watch and covet the throne.</p><p>As she has become the glass-half-empty, right-leaning-affiliated version (Clark is the glass-half-full version) of the fight the WNBA refuses to fight. Soon to be the W’s Kristi Noem (former ICE Barbie, president enforcer, etc.) if Sophie’s not careful.</p><p>What Sophie Cunningham’s ‘‘rock star’’ ascension says about us is less important than what it can and more than likely will say about her. The impact, support, thirst, enthusiasm, excitement and power all bestowed on her — and now through her — with reason will ultimately dictate what she’ll eventually stand to represent. As long as she’s cool with knowing both what and whom she’s about to become.</p><p>Because Barbies, we all know, can be a toy or a weapon.<br></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Sister makes being around her an unpleasant experience
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My unpleasant older sister lives by the creed, "It's my way or the highway." As a result, she has no close friends, no husband or partner, no social circle. She was "strongly encouraged" to take early retirement from teaching because she couldn't get along with her co-workers.</p><p>After retirement, she joined a few clubs but soon quit because they "didn't do things right," aka her way. Even though she treats me terribly, I have tried for years to be the better person and invite her to my family gatherings so she doesn't have to spend holidays alone.</p><p>Unfortunately, she is also the world's worst houseguest. Within minutes of arriving, she announces a list of things she just can't stand (and are therefore prohibited during her stay). These include certain TV shows, music, foods, ingredients, topics of conversation, any family story that includes her, etc. She stays until everyone has gone and then berates me for everything that I did wrong during her visit.</p><p>If I don't invite her, I feel guilty that she's alone and has no other options. If I do invite her, I'm so stressed that I don't get to enjoy having time with my children and grandchildren, which is very precious to me. What do you recommend I do? — <i>TORN SISTER IN WASHINGTON</i></p><p><b>DEAR SISTER:</b> I think you have suffered enough. If you decide to invite your older sister to visit again, first establish some ground rules. The first should be that when she's under your roof, you, not she, will decide on what entertainment is appropriate and what foods you will serve. And how they're prepared. No topic of discussion will be off-limits. If there is something she can't eat, she can refuse it. If something being talked about is not to her liking, she's free to leave the room.</p><p>The second ground rule should be that you are not obligated to entertain her 24/7, particularly if you want to spend time with the grandchildren.</p><p>Of course, Sissy is free to reject your kind invitation, but if she accepts your conditions, the holiday will be a far happier one for you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> My husband passed away last year. I live by myself in a two-story house with three bedrooms and three bathrooms. My kids want me to sell it. I don't care for the stairs, but that's the only thing I don't like about my house. I've lived in this house for more than 30 years, and I don't want to sell. I've always done what everybody else, especially my husband, has told me to do. For once in my life, I want to do what I want to do. Can you give me some advice? — <i>FINALLY FREE</i></p><p><b>DEAR FREE:</b> My advice is to take your own advice. You seem to be happy where you are, so don't allow your kids to pressure you into selling before you're ready. I will add, though, that it would be wise to run your kids' worries by your physician. If there are health concerns that make it unsafe for you to live alone in a big house with stairs, it's best to listen to your doctor.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren, also known as Jeanne Phillips, and was founded by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 69440, Los Angeles, CA 90069.</i></p><p>To receive a collection of Abby's most memorable — and most frequently requested — poems and essays, send your name and mailing address, plus check or money order for $8 (U.S. funds), to: Dear Abby — Keepers Booklet, P.O. Box 446, Kings Mills, OH 45034-0446. (Shipping and handling are included in the price.)</p>

entries.title: Furniture to tech: Lithuania's economy a bright spot amid Trump's tariffs
entries.summary: <p>KLAIPĖDA, Lithuania — The Trump administration's tariffs increased prices for consumers and companies in Chicago and around the world, but Jurgita Radzevičė's business has a cushion, thanks to some lucky timing.</p><p>SBA Home, a Lithuanian furniture maker that supplies items for Ikea, opened a highly automated 500,000-square-foot factory last fall in Mocksville, North Carolina, outside Winston-Salem.</p><p>Radzevičė, the 45-year-old CEO of SBA Home, says even though the project was years in the making, the timing was perfect.</p><p>The $70 million facility opened months after President Donald Trump announced his so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/money/2025/04/02/trump-liberation-day-tariffs-manufacturing-inflation-trade-wars" target="_blank" >“Liberation Day” tariffs</a> in April 2025, which included a 20% tax on imports from the European Union. The U.S. Supreme Court <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/economy/2026/02/20/supreme-court-trump-sweeping-tariffs-john-roberts-economic-agenda" target="_blank" >ruled the tariffs illegal</a> in February, but Trump recently announced a new tariff plan that will levy 10% on EU goods.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> Ikea has a large branded factory in Kazlų Rūda, a town of about 5,400 people in a forested area southwest of Kaunas.</p><p>Mantas Varaška, mayor of Kazlų Rūda, says the U.S. tariffs upended established trading relationships and harmed everyone.</p><p>"It makes all the world unstable, including those small countries like Lithuania or other Baltic countries," Varaška, 47, says.</p><p>Companies like Ikea plan several years ahead for production and logistics, including shipping by rail, trucks and planes.</p><p>"So, imagine how it changes the traffic, especially because of American tax decisions, when … Ikea has to rethink all its producing strategy for three years. And of course, it affects us because if there are some changes going in production lines, in technology equipment, they are interrupting the production work for two months, for three months, they are [downsizing to] one shift. That means that people are losing their jobs, or that people are receiving less money for two or three months," he says.</p><p>Radzevičė says between the tariffs and increased oil prices from the Iran War, "nobody is giving you any time to prepare. That means this is the new normal in our business environment — you need to be extremely fast, extremely dynamic."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" Silicon Valley</h3><p>Lithuania's economy took off after it joined the EU. By 2007, its gross domestic product was growing by 11.1% a year, according to the World Bank Group.</p><p>Growth has slowed in recent years to around 3%, but foreign investment continues to pour in.</p><p>While Lithuania has a long history of furniture-making, thanks to its pine, spruce and birch forests covering about one-third of its land, it's also known for fintech startups and laser production.</p><p>The country of 2.8 million people has six unicorn companies, or businesses valued at more than $1 billion, and its capital Vilnius is called the Baltic Silicon Valley. </p><p>"We're a small country, so we can't really mass-produce something for the entire world. We just don't have the capacity. But services is where we are really good, and financial services is one of them," says Tadas Vizgirda, 57, managing director of payment processor Shift4 Payments.</p><div class="Enhancement" He says the fintech sector took off about 10 years ago, when Lithuania loosened its banking rules and international companies found a highly educated population with young workers who speak English.</p><p>"We are a small nation that is just super positive. We're glowing," he says.</p><p>Edvinas Grikšas, Lithuania's minister for economy and innovation, says the country long ago shed its image as a cheap labor company.</p><p>"We are becoming a technology-based, high added value-based country," he says.</p><p>At 35, Grikšas is the youngest member of the governing cabinet. He's proud of its tech sector and its growing artificial intelligence presence. His ministry has a "3i" strategy, meaning innovation, investments and institutions. </p><p>It could soon add a fourth "i": India.</p><p>The EU and India recently reached a free trade agreement, and Lithuanian access to India's market of 1.4 billion people could make up for some of the trade hiccups caused by the U.S.</p><p>"Cooperation with India is very important and not only in traditional industry," Grikšas says. "They are very interested in our laser sector, in our biotechnology achievement, gene therapy. We are among the top countries globally in those kinds of achievements."</p><p>But Grikšas is mindful of Lithuania's less urban areas, where more traditional industries still hold sway. The country's goal is to send at least 30% of government investment toward less developed regions.</p><p>"We see this as an opportunity to grow, to raise all our economy — not only in the biggest entries.title: 3 people fatally shot on South Side in overnight violence
entries.summary: <p>Three people were killed in overnight violence across the South Side.</p><p>A 24-year-old woman in Roseland, a 61-year-old man in Englewood and a male victim in South Chicago were killed in under three hours early Sunday, according to Chicago police. Six people were also shot in Humboldt Park, and two victims are in critical condition.</p><p>No one has been arrested for any of the violence, according to police.</p><p>The woman in Roseland was outside with a large group just before 1 a.m. Sunday in the 10400 block of South Michigan Avenue when someone fired shots into the crowd, police said. The woman and a 20-year-old woman were both struck. The 20-year-old was taken in good condition to Roseland Hospital. The other woman was taken to University of Chicago Medical Center where she was later pronounced dead.</p><p>About 15 minutes later, the 61-year-old man was found with a fatal gunshot wound to his back at around 1:05 a.m. in the 5600 block of South Racine Avenue. Police did not share any additional details.</p><p>Just after 3 a.m., the male victim and a 32-year-old woman were outside in the 8900 block of South Escanaba Avenue when they heard and felt gunshots, police said. The woman took herself to Trinity Hospital in good condition. The male victim, whose age has not been reported, was shot in the neck and taken to University of Chicago where he was later pronounced dead.</p><p>In Humboldt Park, a gunman fired shots into a group of people around 2 a.m. Sunday in the 900 block of North Central Park Avenue, police said. Six people were injured. Two men are in critical condition after both suffered several gunshot wounds: a 35-year-old man taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center and a 36-year-old man taken to Mount Sinai Hospital.</p><p>The four other victims are in good condition at several hospitals: a 33-year-old man at Humboldt Park Health, a 34-year-old woman at Mount Sinai, a 39-year-old man at Stroger Hospital and a 46-year-old woman also at Stroger.</p>

entries.title: Bears must back up offseason talk, especially on offense, with sharp start to training camp this week
entries.summary: <p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> were fairly quiet when it came to expectations a year ago, coming off a disastrous season and a hard reset at head coach with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> replacing Matt Eberflus. They seemed to learn a tough lesson after launching the 2024 season with “Hard Knocks” in what came across as a pre-celebration of success.</p><p>There’s been a little more chatter this year, though.</p><p>The Bears earned the right to voice high expectations after going 11-6 and winning a playoff game last season, and the logical next step from there is to establish themselves as a legitimate contender, but it’s never automatic. Regression, personnel misjudgments and injuries lurk as pitfalls for any team.</p><p>After a relatively quiet offseason, most of the talk at Halas Hall has been about improvement coming from within the existing roster. By nature, that’s all projection, and they need to produce some proof.</p><p>The Bears’ big ambitions hinge predominantly on the potential rise of quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, who did a lot of great things last season but still has a lot to sharpen. They’re counting on having the best tight end group in the NFL, some unexpected patches on the offensive line holding steady and second-year wide receiver Luther Burden becoming an elite playmaker.</p><p>On the other side of the ball, they believe they can fix their pass-rush problems with better coaching and the emergence of defensive ends Dayo Odeyingbo (17 1/2 career sacks in 69 games), Austin Booker (six in 27) and Shemar Turner (second-round pick who played just five games as a rookie due to injury).</p><p>That’s only optimism until they show results, and those should be evident early in training camp. The Bears report Tuesday and start practice Wednesday, and likely will begin more intense sessions Aug. 3.</p><p>One of the biggest talking points in the building has been that the offense will be ready to roll immediately now that Williams and others are fully versed in Johnson’s offense.</p><p>“We can hit the ground running a little bit from an offensive perspective,” Johnson said during Organized Team Activities.</p><p>That starts with Williams, at this stage of his partnership with Johnson and in his career overall, running the show so authoritatively that he can correct any errors by teammates. From the beginning of camp, it should look significantly different than it did a year ago, when Johnson was all over him for pre-snap missteps and delay-of-game penalties. The team’s 10th practice was so “sloppy,” Johnson said, that it’d be impossible to win many games unless it got dramatically better.</p><p>Williams also should look sharper as a passer from the jump. When Johnson set the bar at 70 percent completions last year, he specified that it applied not only to the season at large, but to every day of practice.</p><p>Johnson said the coaching staff is putting a letter grade on literally every throw Williams makes, and while he wouldn’t reveal his report card at the end of minicamp last month, he said only, “It’s been OK.”</p><p>Williams completed just 58.1 percent of his passes last season, which was last in the league among players who threw at least 250 passes and the lowest by a Bears quarterback in more than a decade.</p><p>It’s hard to tell where Williams stands on that. In one sense, it’s merely one statistic by a player who set the franchise passing record, produced insane highlights and led the Bears to their first playoff win in 15 years. In another, it’s a vital part of the equation for an efficient, consistent passing attack.</p><p>Johnson undoubtedly would lean toward the latter. Williams has agreed with his coach on that point multiple times, but also seemed casual about it in an appearance on “Pardon My Take” this summer, saying, “We’ll get it up just to shut everybody up and… make everybody’s heart feel warm and lovely. He added an acknowledgment that it would significantly help the offense overall.</p><p>None of the last 10 All-Pro quarterbacks had a completion percentage under 65. All nine teams ahead of the Bears in passing yardage last season completed at least 64% of their passes. It matters.</p><p>Beyond Williams, the first week of training camp will be a great indication of how well Burden grasps the playbook. Johnson said he’s “buying Luther Burden stock right now” at the end of May, and it’s likely he’d only make a comment like that if Burden was on top of his job. If he’s shaky this week, that’s a concern.</p><p>Many other areas will be difficult to fully evaluate until full-contact practices are underway. That’s when it becomes clear how strong the offensive and defensive lines are, as well as what the Bears have in the running game with D’Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai.</p><p>The main goal for now is to pick up where they left off offensively. Everything should be clear in the huddle. All the pre-snap motion should be clockwork. Delay-of-game flags shouldn’t happen. Routes should be crisp, and passes should be sharp. It’s time to back up the talk.</p>
entries.author: Jason Lieser

entries.title: 3 killed after car fleeing authorities drives off bridge, crashes into train box car in Bedford Park
entries.summary: <p>Three people were killed early Sunday after a car fleeing police drove off a bridge and into a train box car in Bedford Park, Chicago police said. A fourth passenger is in critical condition.</p><p>Chicago police were responding to a call after someone pointed a gun at a person from the car. Officers tried to pull over the vehicle, but the driver didn't stop. Officers briefly chased the car before stopping the pursuit, according to police.</p><p>Illinois State Police troopers then saw the same car and attempted to stop it in the 5500 block of South Cicero Avenue. The car briefly stopped for the troopers, but then the driver sped off again. State troopers radioed Chicago police for back up.</p><p>The wanted car — speeding away from police in the 6900 block of South Cicero Avenue — drove off a bridge and crashed into a train box car at around 2:15 a.m. Sunday, police said. Two men and one woman in the car were killed and pronounced dead at the scene. A second woman was taken to Christ Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No other injuries were reported. Chicago police are investigating the incident with assistance from state police.</p>

entries.summary: <p>St. Vincent walked away from her Chicago Symphony Orchestra debut Saturday night with even more fan appreciation … and a friendship bracelet.</p><p>After an hour building up a great deal of poise and repose behind the reworked material from her catalog, St. Vincent, whose birth name is Annie Clark, broke through the orchestral fourth wall to rile up the reverent crowd and launch them out of their seats in Ravinia’s Hunter Pavilion.</p><p>Strutting down the aisles while singing a few lines from former collaborator Sufjan Stevens’ “Chicago,” she nuzzled security guards’ heads, nearly suffocated someone in the front row with a tight embrace (“you just got a whole lot of breast sweat”) and happily took the bracelet decorated with beads that spelled out “Annie Clark” In time, she’s proved herself as much of a vocal powerhouse as a guitar master, with her own signature line. class="Figure-credit"><p>Timothy Hiatt/For the Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The appearance at Ravinia (her first since taking the stage with Byrne in 2013) follows a series of collaborations with local orchestras this summer, also including stops at the Detroit Opera House, Atlanta Symphony Hall, Wolf Trap National Park in Virginia and Interlochen in Michigan.</p><p>It also follows a trail of pop and rock stars who have been flirting with orchestras as of late, with Ravinia taking a spotlight locally. Just a few weeks ago, Lizzo paired up with the CSO for the park’s 2026 grand opening. But witnessing St. Vincent performing alongside the orchestra felt less of a trend and more like she had been incubating on it all along.</p><p>The idea originally spawned from Clark’s invitation to BBC Proms at London’s Royal Albert Hall last fall, which begat the well-received “Live in London!” album released earlier this year. Thankfully, she wasn’t done with the project, wanting to bring it to audiences around the country.</p><p>Working with conductor Jules Buckley and her touring keyboardist Rachel Eckroth, aka “the woman who made this all happen,” Clark rearranged more than a dozen of her songs to channel the depth and grandeur of a symphony. She also brought along a traditional rock ensemble — guitarist Robert Ellis, bassist Allee Fütterer and drummer John Hadfield — to create an incredibly unique crossover that appealed to both rock and classical bases.</p><p>The added swell of strings on “Violent Times” (from 2024 album “All Born Screaming”) brought out its intense noir, making a case for a “James Bond” theme song placement. The chimes and flute on “The Bed” illuminated its soft and wistful nature. And the apocalyptic crescendo of percussion on “Hell Is Near” made you feel like you should probably start praying.</p><p>Clark performed a few songs sans her trusted guitar, which allowed her vocals to dominate. But when she added the electric, it was transcendent. No more so than on “Smoking Section” when her guitar’s wailing cry mixed with strings made the harrowing refrain of “it’s not the end” feel like an actual swan song.</p><p>This performance wasn’t as much about changing the scope of St. Vincent or her music. She dropped all her mother------ on cue in “New York.” She lit up a cigarette during “Los Ageless.” And her feral spiral on the crowd favorite “Digital Witness” — where a close-gripped microphone smeared her red lipstick to make her look downright bloodthirsty — felt like a repeat of the Riot Fest set in 2024.</p><p>Rather, Clark's latest segue is about translating her intense body of work into another language, a romance language, in which she is equally fluent. And by the end of the 85-minute suite, everyone was on their feet again, this time for a deserved standing ovation.<br><b></b></p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/music/2026/07/20/st-vincent-annie-clark-chicago-symphony-orchestra-collaboration" >St. Vincent explores ‘new dimension’ in genre-defying collab with orchestras like Chicago Symphony</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p><h3>Set list for St. Vincent performance with the Chicago Symphony Orchestra at Ravinia July 25, 2026</h3><p>We Put a Pearl in the Ground<br>Hell Is Near<br>Reckless<br>Violent Times<br>Black Rainbow<br>Marrow<br>The Bed<br>Smoking Section<br>Now, Now<br>Live in the Dream<br>The Nowhere Inn<br>Digital Witness<br>Los Ageless<br>New York<br>Paris Is Burning</p><p><b>Encore</b><br>Slow Disco</p>

entries.title: Thunderstorms mixed with heat and humidity move into Chicago area
entries.summary: <p>Temperatures and humidity are rising in Chicago with a chance for thunderstorms to roll into the region Sunday evening and into Monday.</p><p>National Weather Service forecasters say "periods of thunderstorms" are possible Sunday and Monday night, but the exact timing and location are uncertain.</p><p>Hot and humid conditions for Chicago are more of a sure thing, according to the weather service, with temperatures hitting 91 and the heat index pushing 105 for Sunday. Monday's temperatures are expected to be higher at 93, with the potential for a heat index of 110. </p><p>The rest of the week will likely be cooler as temperatures drop to the low 80s, according to the weather service.</p><p>Six people in Cook County <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/environment/2026/07/20/six-heat-related-deaths-in-cook-county-marks-july-as-the-deadliest-month-in-more-than-a-decade" target="_blank" >have died for heat-related reasons</a> so far this summer, marking the deadliest stretch of extreme hot-weather deaths in over a decade.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" > <div class="TweetUrl"> <blockquote class="twitter-tweet"><p lang="en" dir="ltr">Hot & humidity today & Monday will be accompanied by a threat for storms at times tonight thru Monday evening. entries.title: Building emotional intelligence, one cellblock at a time
entries.summary: <p>There’s something unusual happening at the Illinois River Correctional Center.</p><p>For a prison, there’s a lot of talk of community, emotional intelligence, nurturing, support — and it’s not just talk. It’s focused in one wing in the prison — 3-A — but the zeitgeist seems to be spreading. </p><p>The latest episode of <i>Prisoncast!</i> profiles the Building Block program at the prison, which was started up by several guys who'd transferred in from a maximum security prison. These men — some of whom have life sentences — used the college degrees they got in prison to start a program to help others who will have the chance to be released some day.</p><p>"I was afforded the opportunity for education [and] it opened my eyes to my own life and how unhealthy I thought about things...which made me really start asking,'Why did I do the things that I did?'" said one of the program's founders, Yarmale Thomas. "Once people start getting to that then they can start addressing it and begin to heal. Once they heal, they can help others heal around them."</p><p><b>Learn more on <i>Prisoncast!</i>, airing Sunday, July 26th from 2 to 4PM CT on WBEZ 91.5 FM, at wbez.org, and on all Illinois Public Radio stations.</b></p><p>In the first hour of the show, <i>Prisoncast!</i> profiles the Building Block program inside Illinois River Correctional Center. We have an update on the state of health care in Illinois prisons. And, how one incarcerated listener's sound request had us watching peewee hockey on VHS with his parents.</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" entries.title: Bobblehead bopper: White Sox star Munetaka Murakami homers in first at-bat on big day
entries.summary: <p>All-Star Munetaka Murakami has homered in his first at-bat on his bobblehead day Sunday to put the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" target="_blank" >White Sox</a> ahead 2-1 over the Houston Astros. The Sox are trying to avoid being swept.</p><p>The two-run shot to left was Murakami’s 21st of the season. It's the first time he’s gone deep in 12 games since returning from a right hamstring strain he suffered on May 29 and that sidelined him for six weeks.</p><p>Murakami was tied for the major league lead with 20 homers when he suffered the injury running out a grounder.<br></p>
entries.author: Matt Carlson

entries.title: White Sox shortstop Colson Montgomery sits out Sunday with bruised shin
entries.summary: <p>Shortstop Colson Montgomery, who leads the White Sox with 24 homers, sat out Sunday’s 12-3 win over Houston with a bruised right shin. </p><p>He aggravated a previous injury there in the ninth inning of Saturday’s 4-1 loss when he fouled a pitch off his leg, then singled to drive in Chicago’s only run.  </p><p>Montgomery wanted to rest and treat the contusion on Sunday and hopes to be ready to play Monday when the White Sox open a four-game series with the New York Yankees. </p><p>“Kind of things just to flush out, you know, swelling and things like that,” Montgomery said. “It’s just something that, you know, we get ahead of right now.”</p><p>Montgomery said the fouled-off ball struck him above his “regular” and custom leg guards and near a previously bruised area. Injured catcher Kyle Teel suggested adapting a catcher’s shin guard for protection, but Montgomery said it wouldn’t be comfortable.</p><h3><b>Measuring stick?</b></h3><p>The New York Yankees come to the South Side for four games starting Monday, then meet the Cubs at Wrigley Field for three.</p><p>The timing might be perfect for Chicago’s teams.</p><p>New York placed All-Star outfielder and former Cub Cody Bellinger on the IL with a left hamstring strain on Sunday. The Yankees have been without slugger Aaron Judge (fractured rib)since May 31 and DH Giancarlo Stanton (strained right calf) since April 24.</p><p>Still, the Yankees entered Sunday in second place in the AL East and owned the second-best record in the league.</p><p>But White Sox manager Will Venable downplays the upcoming series as a measuring stick for his team</p><p>"I think we're kind of past playing games and measuring where we're at,” Venable said. “We know we're a good team. We know the Yankees are a good team. We'll worry about them when we get there.”</p><h3><b>All-family first pitch</b></h3><p>Munetaka Murakami’s parents both threw out ceremonial first pitches before Sunday’s 12-3 over Houston. Then Murakami hit two homers and recorded a career-best six RBIs.</p><p>The slugger’s father, Kimiya, tossed with Murakami catching. His mother, Fumiyo, threw to interpreter Kenzo Yagi.</p><p>“The last time my parents came, I wasn’t on the field, I was injured,” Murakami said. “Just being out there on the field today and getting the result in front of them, it’s just really speechless.”</p><h3><b>Spritz, that’s it!</b></h3><p>Sunday’s Murakami bobblehead was sponsored by Toto, Ltd, a leading Japanese plumbing fixture brand, and its Toto Washlet. That’s the electronic toilet seat bidet the White Sox asked Toto to install in their clubhouse commodes after Murakami requested it.</p><p>Bidets use a stream of water to clean a person’s, well, derriere. Although “funky” to many Americans, bidets are common in Japan and some European countries.</p><p>Shinya Tamura, the president of Toto, also threw a ceremonial first pitch Sunday, and the company had a product display across from the Rate. The Murakami bobblehead was featured on Toto’s USA website.</p><p>Toto is using its relationship with Murakami to help introduce it Washlet  to U.S. customers, including other MLB teams.</p><p>“It’s not like everyone knows about it yet, “Tamura said through an interpreter. “And having Murakami as a popular person, influential person, introduce something about Washlet Toto, that will will be helpful to us.”</p><div class="PageListL" data-module data-hide-authors="true" data-hide-categories="true" data-hide-dates="true" data-show-loadmore="true" ><a class="AnchorLink" id="list-4a0005" entries.title: Robbins renames Dwyane Wade’s childhood street after the NBA champ, All-Star and hometown hero
entries.summary: <p>Dwyane Wade, a 13-time NBA All-Star and a three-time NBA champion, was once a 5-year-old boy whose dad would take him to play basketball in high school gyms on Friday nights and watch Michael Jordan’s “Come Fly With Me” VHS tape religiously.</p><p>Sunday afternoon, he added yet another accolade to his list, seven years after retiring from the court. But this one was for all the kids still in south suburban Robbins, reflecting his younger self.</p><p>His hometown renamed the street he grew up on after him, unveiling the signs at a ceremony Sunday. Not just honorarily either — South Claire Boulevard is now Dwyane Wade Boulevard.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Dwyane Wade (right) and his father Dwyane Wade Sr. point at the newly unveiled street sign on Sunday. “Before the world ever saw Dwyane Wade, Robbins saw me,” the younger Wade said to the kids in the crowd. “Not the champion or Hall of Famer, just a kid whose family was looking for a chance. … Don’t wait for the world to see you; see yourself first and believe in you.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“How do you put into words what it feels like to be honored on a street that helped raise you?” Wade asked the crowd. “I’ve been blessed with a life I never could’ve imagined. … But standing here today, seeing familiar faces, being on this street I’ve run up and down so many times, it feels different than anywhere else I’ve been in this world.”</p><p>Wade chose to follow his brother to the local Richards High School as opposed to Chicago’s Whitney Young, which is known for fostering basketball talent. He went on to lead Marquette University to the Final Four before being drafted fifth overall in 2003.</p><p>He spent most of his 16-year career with the Heat, along with stints on the Chicago Bulls and Cleveland Cavaliers before retiring in 2019. He racked up numerous team records and an Olympic gold medal as Team USA’s leading scorer in 2008.</p><p>All of this culminated in his induction into the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bulls/2023/8/12/23830082/dwyane-wade-hall-of-fame-speech-full-induction-chicago-richards-robbins-bulls-heat-allen-iverson" target="_blank" ><u>NBA Hall of Fame in 2023</u></a>, and now, his childhood street being renamed after him.</p><p>Rock Flemings showed up to the event wearing his college jersey, which Wade later signed for her. She said it was the closest she could get to his high school jersey, the only one she doesn’t own.</p><p>The Philadelphia resident had been in town for the WNBA All-Star weekend, but knew she had to be there to see a player who influenced her own style on the court.</p><p>“He was just a different player,” Flemings said. “Now I just wish he’d come back and play in Philly with LeBron [James].”</p><p>The sign has meaning beyond sporting success, though, Wade said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a I could do what he did or better. I just have to prove myself.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Candace Dane Chambers/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Brenae Stewart, a former cheerleader with the Robbins Eagles program and now a hip-hop dancer, attended with her mom and younger brother. I could do what he did or better. I just have to prove myself.”</p><p>Gywon Garth, a born and raised Robbins resident, arrived wearing the jersey he bought shortly after Wade was drafted in 2003.</p><p>Garth is still local and works in construction.
