entries.title: Cubs will discuss whether Jameson Taillon makes next start after he gets rocked again: ‘I’m hurting the team’
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH – Things have gone from bad to worse for <b>Jameson Taillon</b>.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ veteran righty hasn’t figured out how to keep the ball in the yard this season, tagged for three more home runs Sunday, jacking his season total up to 25. He allowed seven runs in an 8-7 loss to the Pirates.</p><p>“We need better than that,” manager <b>Craig Counsell</b> said.</p><p>The Cubs are 1-7 in the last eight games Taillon has started.</p><p>It’s reached the point where team brass has to figure out whether he’ll make his next start.</p><p>“I think we’ve got to discuss it,” Counsell said. “We’ve got days to figure that out. But we’ve got to discuss what’s best for the staff, in general.”</p><p>The stakes are high. The Cubs can’t afford to keep sending Taillon to the mound in the state he’s in, not <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >in the thick of a playoff race</a> and seven games behind the division-leading Brewers.</p><p>Though Taillon was big for the Cubs last postseason, the type of pitcher he’s been lately – he’s got an 8.90 ERA in his last seven starts – is not the type of pitcher you can trot out in a playoff game.</p><p>He knows it.</p><p>“It hasn’t been very good, and the results speak for themselves,” he said. “I’m confident I can figure it out, but when you’re going out there and hurting the team, it’s obviously not a good place to be.</p><p>“I feel like the work’s good, and then I go out there and kind of revert back to what I’ve been doing. The work’s been good. … I’m just not seeing it pay off right now.</p><p>“I’ve been around long enough to know that I’m hurting the team and have been for a little while now. I’m not naive to that at all.”</p><p>Complicating things, the Cubs are still dogged by pitching injuries. Until recently, Taillon’s hamstring strain was one of them, sidelining him for a month and a half. They need innings.</p><p>But with the trade deadline just a week away, <b>Jed Hoyer</b>’s front office <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >will be pursuing pitching</a>, needing to land an impact arm or two to prevent a repeat of last year, when depth issues contributed to the team’s postseason exit.</p><p>Taillon’s struggles have only emphasized that need. There’s a lot of season left for him to iron things out, but the way he’s pitching right now should have Hoyer looking for a potential replacement before time runs out on Aug. 3.</p><p><b>More starts for Assad?</b></p><p>Might right-hander <b>Javier Assad</b> return to the rotation after his last two appearances came in relief?</p><p>That would figure to be among the factors in the team’s decision-making while discussing what to do with Taillon.</p><p>Before Sunday’s game, Counsell said that while the team was planning a five-man rotation absent Assad during a stretch of 17 games in 17 days – utilizing Assad’s versatility to spell bullpen arms – there could be more starts in his future.</p><p>“Essentially, we’re keeping Javy – I don’t want to say ‘fresh’ – but he gets a little break [from starting] here,” Counsell said. “So if we need to count on him for a stretch, you feel really good having to do that. I would guess there’s going to be more starts for him.”</p><p><b>Optimism for injured pitchers</b></p><p>The Cubs are seeing progress in the injury recoveries of righty relievers and free-agent signees <b>Hunter Harvey</b> and <b>Shelby Miller</b>.</p><p>Harvey, should all go well, could go on a minor league rehab assignment as soon as early August, while Counsell said it’s possible Miller could pitch for the big league team before season’s end.</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: Pete Crow-Armstrong says any trade-deadline adds will only help Cubs, but ‘I love what we’ve got’
entries.summary: <p>PITTSBURGH – Pete Crow-Armstrong knows what happens at this time of year.</p><p>He knows additions are likely coming the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a>’ way at the trade deadline.</p><p>That’s what happened last year, even if fans were underwhelmed by the multiple moves Jed Hoyer’s front office made, work that was particularly colored after the fact by the team’s briefer-than-hoped stay in the postseason.</p><p>Whether Hoyer <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/22/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-jed-hoyer-pitching-nico-hoerner-buyers-nl-central-standings-brewers" >decides to go big or makes smaller moves</a> that earn gripes from the fan base, there will almost surely be newcomers on the Cubs’ roster come Aug. 4, the day after the deadline.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/02/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-mvp-player-of-the-month-june-stats-babe-ruth-lou-gehrig-shohei-ohtani" >the MVP candidate</a> who hopes to achieve this team’s championship-level goals as much as anyone, is ready for it.</p><p>He’s also ready to see what this group can do when the lights get really, really bright in October.</p><p>What’s his outlook for the rest of the season?</p><p>“I love this team,” he said after a four-hit game in Saturday’s win over the Pirates. “That’s my outlook. … I love who’s in this clubhouse, just because every single person in here has shown they’re up for the challenge.</p><p>“If we go get pieces, that’s only going to help us, because of the way that we’re playing and what we’re capable of as this current clubhouse. There are a lot of big things that we can achieve with this group.”</p><p>It’s hard to argue with what the Cubs have been doing; they’ve got a 25-12 record since June 11.</p><p>Coming into Sunday, no team had scored more runs (226), drawn more walks (161), reached base at a higher clip (.351) than the Cubs in that span.</p><p>Add in the Gold Glove defense <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/24/game-saving-defense-fires-up-cubs-in-thick-of-division-race-were-at-that-point-every-game-matters" >that’s winning games</a> and a pitching staff that’s getting contributions from both expected and unexpected sources, and the Cubs have recently looked like what their record says they are: one of the best teams in baseball.</p><p>Crow-Armstrong, of course, has been at the heart of it all, combining home-run barrages with dramatically improved on-base skills and best-in-baseball defense in center field. As of Sunday morning, his 7.0 fWAR was far and away the most among position players.</p><p>Yet, with all that’s going well – even with the team still dogged by pitching injuries – there could be a lot riding on what Hoyer & Co. do (or don’t do) at the trade deadline, and all eyes will be on the Cubs’ front office, with fans hoping its work solidifies this team as a championship contender.</p><p>That work <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/17/cubs-mlb-trade-deadline-rumors-starting-pitching-jed-hoyer-front-office" >figures to focus on pitching</a>, a need emphasized after veteran righty Jameson Taillon got rocked Sunday in an 8-7 loss to the Pirates. He gave up three more home runs to jack his season total up to 25; only one pitcher in baseball started the day with more dingers allowed.</p><p>The Cubs have lost all but one of the last eight games he’s started.</p><p>Hoyer has talked up a position-player group he believes can win a lot of games in October. But it’s tough to win in October with a starter giving up multiple home runs each time out, adding to the team’s need.</p><p>A year ago, the Cubs’ pitching depth was part of the reason they were ushered out of the playoffs by the Brewers. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/07/25/cubs-playoffs-brewers-pirates-nl-central-matthew-boyd-starting-rotation" >Chasing that same Brewers team</a> in the NL Central standings, an influx of pitching would go a long way toward stabilizing an injury-ravaged staff, a necessity if the depth is going to be there this year.</p><p>But any additions could still be as far as a week away.</p><p>In the meantime, Crow-Armstrong and the Cubs are excited about embarking on the road to the World Series with the guys currently in Cubs uniforms, the ones who will most likely be driving the bus to what they hope is late October.</p><p>“Whatever the front office does, I assume it’ll probably just help our cause,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I’m excited to welcome anybody that finds themselves in a Cub uniform. But for now and until the deadline, I love what we’ve got, and I love what we’re doing.”</p>
